final_answer:
**Direct answer:** No. WAL doesn't eliminate write contention. Only one writer can be active at a time, and a second writer still has to wait or fail with `SQLITE_BUSY`. WAL's concurrency benefit is that readers and the single writer no longer block each other. It also makes commits cheaper.

**Claims and sources**

- WAL allows only one writer at a time, because there is one WAL file. Readers can proceed during a write.
  https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- Readers don't block writers, and writers don't block readers. Each reader sees a consistent snapshot taken at the start of its transaction. Writers only append to the WAL.
  https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- In the older rollback-journal mode, only one connection can hold the RESERVED lock (the write intent) at a time. A second writer that can't get it gets `SQLITE_BUSY`. Readers can keep reading while RESERVED is held, but a writer needs an EXCLUSIVE lock to write to the database file. So WAL's gain is mostly in reader/writer overlap, not in writer/writer concurrency. The lockingv3 page describes rollback-journal mode only, so I'm inferring from that page that WAL's own single-writer rule is the equivalent limit. The WAL page states that rule directly.
  https://www.sqlite.org/lockingv3.html

- WAL is "significantly faster in most scenarios." Writes are faster because content is written once instead of twice, I/O is more sequential, and there are far fewer `fsync()` calls. This shortens how long the write lock is held, but it doesn't remove the lock.
  https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- WAL has costs:
  - It may be about 1–2% slower for read-mostly workloads.
  - All processes must be on the same host, so it doesn't work over a network filesystem.
  - It works best with small transactions.
  - Checkpoints are an extra operation to manage.
  
  https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- Checkpoint starvation can happen. If there are always overlapping readers, the checkpoint never completes and the WAL grows without bound. Larger WALs also slow reads.
  https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- Even with a busy handler or `busy_timeout` set, SQLite may return `SQLITE_BUSY` immediately when waiting could deadlock. The documented example is a connection holding a read lock that is trying to promote to a write lock, while another connection holds the write lock. Applications must still handle `SQLITE_BUSY`.
  https://www.sqlite.org/c3ref/busy_handler.html

- `PRAGMA busy_timeout` sets how many milliseconds a connection waits on a lock.
  https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_busy_timeout

**Not established by these sources:** The suggestion that `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` avoids the read-to-write upgrade failure is common advice, but I didn't verify it in any page I retrieved. The pragma page I fetched was truncated, so I didn't read the last 251 characters. I also didn't find a measured throughput comparison under write-heavy load, so I can't give numbers for how much WAL helps there.

Sources:
- https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/lockingv3.html
- https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_busy_timeout
- https://www.sqlite.org/c3ref/busy_handler.html
